title: Scaling to four GPUs
text: Section 5 of 7

title: Scaling to four GPUs
text:
5.1 Data parallelism
So far, we’ve trained on one GPU, but each Isambard-AI node has four. The simplest way to use all four is called data parallelism.


Each GPU gets its own copy of the model.
Each batch is shared out between the GPUs. With a batch of 64 and four GPUs, each GPU gets 16 images.
Each GPU works out how the model should change, using its own 16 images. These changes are called gradients.
The GPUs average their gradients. They do this by sending data directly to each other, using an NVIDIA library called NCCL, in a step called an all-reduce.
Each GPU updates its copy of the model with the averaged gradients, so all four copies stay the same.

title: Scaling to four GPUs
text:
5.2 What’s happening behind the scenes
PyTorch does this using Distributed Data Parallel (DDP). DDP runs a separate Python process for each GPU, and gives each process a number from 0 to 3, called its rank.






Going deeper: how Ultralytics starts the processes





Your notebook is only one Python process, so Ultralytics gets round this by writing a short training script and running four copies of it, one per GPU, with PyTorch’s torch.distributed.run command. Look for a line starting with DDP: in the output, which shows the exact command it used.
If you run nvidia-smi in a terminal while it’s training, you’ll see four Python processes, one on each GPU.

title: Scaling to four GPUs
text:
5.3 Train on four GPUs
The only thing we change is device=[0, 1, 2, 3].


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

model = YOLO(WEIGHTS)

start = time.perf_counter()
model.train(
    data=str(SPLIT_DIR),
    epochs=EPOCHS,
    imgsz=IMG_SIZE,
    batch=BATCH,  # the total batch is shared out: 64 / 4 = 16 images per GPU
    workers=WORKERS,
    device=[0, 1, 2, 3],  # four GPUs
    project=str(RUNS_DIR),
    name="4gpu",
    exist_ok=True,
    seed=42,
)
time_4gpu = time.perf_counter() - start
print(f"Training on 4 GPUs took {time_4gpu / 60:.1f} minutes")

title: Scaling to four GPUs
text:
5.4 Was it faster?


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

timings = pd.DataFrame(
    {"minutes": [time_1gpu / 60, time_4gpu / 60]},
    index=["1 GPU", "4 GPUs"],
)
timings["speed-up"] = (time_1gpu / 60 / timings["minutes"]).round(2)
print(timings.round(2))

ax = timings["minutes"].plot(kind="barh", color=["#b895ce", "#3d0251"], title="Training time on 1 and 4 GPUs")
perfect = ax.axvline(time_1gpu / 60 / 4, color="grey", linestyle="--", label="Perfect 4x speed-up")
ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], labels=[f"{s:.1f}x" for s in timings["speed-up"]], padding=4)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, timings["minutes"].max() * 1.2)
plt.xlabel("Minutes")
plt.legend(handles=[perfect])
plt.show()

Each bar shows how long a run took, and the number at the end is its speed-up compared with 1 GPU. The dashed line shows where the 4-GPU bar would end if four GPUs were exactly four times faster. The gap between the end of the 4-GPU bar and the dashed line is the time spent on the extra work that comes with using several GPUs.
It almost certainly wasn’t four times faster. There are a few reasons for this:

It takes time to start four processes and connect the GPUs to each other, and for a short training run that’s a large part of the total time.
After every batch, the GPUs have to stop and share their gradients.
The CPU workers now have to load images for four GPUs instead of one.

With a small model and dataset like ours, these costs can cancel out most of the benefit of the extra GPUs. With large models and datasets that take hours or days to train, they matter much less, and more GPUs can make a big difference.

title: Scaling to four GPUs
section: 5.5 Is the model just as good?
text:
5.5 Is the model just as good?


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

true, pred = evaluate(RUNS_DIR / "4gpu" / "weights" / "best.pt")
print(classification_report(true, pred, digits=3))

ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(true, pred, cmap="Purples")
plt.title("4 GPUs: test set")
plt.show()

The results should be close to the 1-GPU model’s, but not exactly the same. The images are shuffled differently and each batch is shared out between the GPUs, so the training doesn’t follow exactly the same path. With only 108 fractures in the test set, a difference of a few fractures found or missed is within normal run-to-run variation.

title: Meet FracAtlas
text:
Section 3 of 7
Before training a model, it’s worth spending some time getting to know the data. In this section we’ll load the labels, look at some of the images and split the data into training, validation and test sets. None of this needs a GPU.

title: Meet FracAtlas
text:
3.1 Load the labels


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "dataset.csv")
print(df.shape)
df.head()

There’s one row for each image, and df.shape shows that there are 4,083 rows.

title: Meet FracAtlas
text:
3.2 How balanced are the classes?


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

counts = df["fractured"].value_counts().rename({0: "Not fractured", 1: "Fractured"})
print(counts)
print(f"\n{df['fractured'].mean():.1%} of images show a fracture")
print(f"{(df['fractured'] == 0).mean():.1%} of images don't show a fracture")

counts.plot(kind="bar", color=["#b895ce", "#3d0251"], rot=0, title="FracAtlas: images per class")
plt.xlabel("Class")
plt.ylabel("Number of images")
plt.show()

Only about 1 in 6 of the images shows a fracture. Data like this is called imbalanced, and we have to be careful about how we judge a model trained on it, which we’ll come back to in section 4.

title: Meet FracAtlas
text:
3.3 Find the image files
The images are in two folders, images/Fractured and images/Non_fractured. This function works out where each image is from its row in the table, and we add the result as a new column.


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

def image_path(row):
    folder = "Fractured" if row["fractured"] == 1 else "Non_fractured"
    return DATA_DIR / "images" / folder / row["image_id"]

df["path"] = df.apply(image_path, axis=1)
print("All image files found:", df["path"].map(Path.exists).all())

title: Meet FracAtlas
text:
3.4 Look at some examples


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(14, 7))
for row_axes, label, title in zip(axes, [1, 0], ["Fractured", "Not fractured"]):
    sample = df[df["fractured"] == label].sample(4, random_state=1)
    for ax, (_, row) in zip(row_axes, sample.iterrows()):
        ax.imshow(Image.open(row["path"]), cmap="gray")
        ax.set_title(f"{title}\n{row['image_id']}", fontsize=9)
        ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Some of the fractures are easy to see. Others are hard to find even when you know they’re there.






A note about this copy of the data



87 of the non-fractured images in the FracAtlas download are slightly damaged: the end of each file is missing. When these images are opened, some of them show the missing part as a flat grey band along the bottom. Because only non-fractured images have the band, a model could learn that “grey band means not fractured”, which has nothing to do with bones.
We’ve cropped the grey bands off and repaired the files in the copy we’re using, and listed the changes in FracAtlas/truncated-images.txt. Problems like this are common in real datasets, so it’s always worth checking your images before training on them.

title: Meet FracAtlas
text:
3.5 How big are the images?


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

sizes = [Image.open(p).size for p in df["path"].sample(200, random_state=1)]
sizes = pd.DataFrame(sizes, columns=["width", "height"])
sizes.describe().round()

Look at the widths and heights in the table. The model needs every image to be the same size. When it tests an image, it scales it until the shorter side is 512 pixels, then keeps the middle 512 × 512 square, so for a tall image a little is cut off the top and bottom. During training it also crops and flips the images at random, so the model sees slightly different versions each epoch.
Choosing the size is a trade-off. Smaller images train faster, but fine details such as hairline fractures can get lost. In our dry run, 224 × 224 pixels with only 10 epochs trained in 30 seconds, but the model found far fewer of the fractures than 512 × 512 pixels with 50 epochs.

title: Meet FracAtlas
text:
3.6 Fractures by body region


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

regions = ["hand", "leg", "hip", "shoulder"]
region_stats = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "images": [df[r].sum() for r in regions],
        "fractured": [df.loc[df[r] == 1, "fractured"].sum() for r in regions],
    },
    index=regions,
)
region_stats["% fractured"] = (100 * region_stats["fractured"] / region_stats["images"]).round(1)
region_stats

title: Meet FracAtlas
text:
3.7 Split the data
We split the images into three sets: training (70%), validation (15%) and test (15%).

The model learns from the training set.
After each epoch, we check how the model is doing on the validation set.
We keep the test set aside until the very end, to see how well the model does on images it has never seen.

stratify=df["fractured"] keeps the same proportion of fractured images in each set, and random_state=42 means we get the same split every time we run the cell.


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

train_df, temp_df = train_test_split(
    df, test_size=0.3, stratify=df["fractured"], random_state=42
)
val_df, test_df = train_test_split(
    temp_df, test_size=0.5, stratify=temp_df["fractured"], random_state=42
)

for name, part in [("train", train_df), ("val", val_df), ("test", test_df)]:
    print(f"{name:5}: {len(part):4} images, {part['fractured'].mean():.1%} fractured")







Can images of the same patient end up in different sets?



With medical images, all the images of one patient should go in the same set. If they don’t, the model can learn to recognise the patient instead of the fracture, and it will look better on the test set than it really is. This is called data leakage.
FracAtlas doesn’t include patient IDs (they were removed to protect patients’ privacy), so we can’t do that here. We know from the multiscan column that some body parts were X-rayed from more than one angle, so some of our test images probably have a matching image in the training set. Bear this in mind when you look at the results, and split by patient whenever your own data lets you.

title: Meet FracAtlas
section: 3.8 Arrange the images for the model
text:
3.8 Arrange the images for the model
The Ultralytics library, which we’ll use to train the model, expects the images to be in one folder per set, with a subfolder for each class:
fracatlas-split/
├── train/
│   ├── fractured/
│   └── not_fractured/
├── val/
│   ├── fractured/
│   └── not_fractured/
└── test/
    ├── fractured/
    └── not_fractured/
Copying all 4,083 images for everyone on the course would take a while and waste space. Instead, we make symbolic links (symlinks), which are tiny files that point to the original images in the shared folder. The model reads them as if they were the images themselves.


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

CLASS_NAMES = {1: "fractured", 0: "not_fractured"}

if SPLIT_DIR.exists():
    shutil.rmtree(SPLIT_DIR)  # start fresh if you re-run this cell (removes the links, not the images)

for split, part in [("train", train_df), ("val", val_df), ("test", test_df)]:
    for _, row in part.iterrows():
        link = SPLIT_DIR / split / CLASS_NAMES[row["fractured"]] / row["image_id"]
        link.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        link.symlink_to(row["path"])

for split in ["train", "val", "test"]:
    for class_dir in sorted((SPLIT_DIR / split).iterdir()):
        print(f"{split}/{class_dir.name}: {len(list(class_dir.iterdir()))} images")

title: Meet FracAtlas
text:
Exercise






Exercise



Add a new cell to the notebook to answer these questions:

How many images show surgical hardware (the hardware column)?
What percentage of those images show a fracture?
Why might hardware cause problems for a fracture classifier?









Show answer





with_hardware = df[df["hardware"] == 1]
print(len(with_hardware), "images show hardware")
print(f"{with_hardware['fractured'].mean():.1%} of them are fractured")
Run the cell to see how many images have hardware, and how many of those are fractured.
Hardware could give the model a shortcut. Plates and screws are bright and easy to spot, and they’re put in after a fracture, so a model might learn that “hardware means fracture” instead of learning what a fracture looks like. Looking for shortcuts like this is an important part of checking whether a medical AI model can be trusted.

title: Why HPC for AI?
text: Section 1 of 7

title: Why HPC for AI?
section: 1.1 Why can’t I just use my laptop?
text:
1.1 Why can’t I just use my laptop?
To train a neural network, we show it thousands of examples, many times over, and after each batch we adjust millions of numbers inside the model (its weights) by a small amount. Most of that work is multiplying large grids of numbers together.

CPU: a small number of fast, flexible cores. It’s good at working through a series of different tasks.
GPU: thousands of simpler cores that all do the same sum on different numbers at once, which is exactly what a neural network needs.

Most laptops have a CPU with only a few cores, and many don’t have a dedicated NVIDIA GPU, which is what most deep learning software is built to use. That’s fine for learning and for small models, but bigger projects soon run into problems. Training can take hours or days, the model or a batch of images might not fit in memory, or you might want to try lots of different settings and not have the time.
This is where HPC systems like Isambard-AI come in. They have many nodes, each with several GPUs and plenty of memory, so you can train models that are too big for your laptop, or train the same model many times to find the best settings.

title: Why HPC for AI?
text:
1.2 Isambard-AI
Isambard-AI is a supercomputer in Bristol, run by the Bristol Centre for Supercomputing (BriCS) as part of the UK’s AI Research Resource. Phase 2 of the system has 1,320 nodes, which are the individual computers that make up the supercomputer. Each node has four NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper “superchips”, and each superchip combines a 72-core Grace CPU with an H100 GPU that has 96 GB of memory.

title: Why HPC for AI?
text:
Exercise






Exercise



Think of a model you’ve trained, or would like to train, in your own work.

Roughly how long does one training run take on the computer you use now?
What limits you most: time, memory, or the number of runs you can do?
If a training run took 10 minutes, what would you do differently?









Show answer





There’s no single right answer, but these are common replies:

Time is the most common limit. If a run takes a day, you can only test one idea a day.
Memory problems usually show up as “CUDA out of memory” errors, or as having to use smaller images or batches than you’d like.
When runs are faster, most people say they’d try more ideas: other models, other settings and more data. This is often the biggest benefit of HPC.

title: HPC for AI - Part 1
text: 4,083 X-rays and four GPUs. Can we teach a computer to spot a fracture?

title: HPC for AI - Part 1
text:
Introduction
In this course you’ll use Isambard-AI, one of the UK’s national supercomputers for AI research, to train a computer vision model.
Training a deep learning model means repeating the same calculations over and over, often millions of times. A laptop can manage this for small problems, but it soon gets too slow. Supercomputers like Isambard-AI are built around GPUs (graphics processing units), which can do thousands of these calculations at the same time. During the course you’ll see how much difference a GPU makes, and what happens when you use more than one.
We’re going to explore this topic using a case study: training a model to spot bone fractures in X-ray images. A model like this could, with a lot more work, help clinicians decide which scans to look at first. This could be useful for patient triage in an emergency department.
Each section of the course starts with a question, and in most sections you’ll answer it by running part of a notebook on Isambard-AI:
Why HPC? → Isambard-AI → The data → 1 GPU → 4 GPUs → Good practice

title: HPC for AI - Part 1
text:
The data: FracAtlas
FracAtlas is a public dataset of 4,083 X-ray images of hands, legs, hips and shoulders. The images were collected from three hospitals in Bangladesh and labelled by two radiologists, and 719 of them show at least one fracture. They have been anonymised and are shared under a CC BY 4.0 licence.
The images come with a file called dataset.csv, which has one row per image. These are the columns we’ll use:







Column
Description




image_id
File name of the image, e.g. IMG0000019.jpg


fractured
1 if the image shows a fracture, 0 if not. This is what we want the model to predict.


hand, leg, hip, shoulder
1 if the image shows that part of the body


hardware
1 if the image shows surgical hardware, such as plates or screws


multiscan
1 if the same body part was X-rayed from more than one angle

text:
How to read this document
The notebook is already written, so you won’t need to type much code. Instead, read each cell before you run it and make sure you know what it’s doing. Once a cell has run, try changing something and running it again; the exercise at the end of each section gives you some ideas. Training the model takes a few minutes each time, so that’s a good moment to ask questions.
Code from the course notebook is shown in a box with the notebook’s name at the top. You’ll find exactly the same code in one of the notebook’s cells:


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

baseline = (test_df["fractured"] == 0).mean()
print(f"Always guessing 'not fractured' would be {baseline:.1%} accurate")

Commands to type into a terminal look like this:


Terminal

nvidia-smi

There’s an exercise at the end of each section, in a blue box. The answer is in the yellow box underneath; have a go yourself before you open it. Green boxes sum up the main points of each section.

title: HPC for AI - Part 1
text:
Intended learning outcomes
By the end of this course, you will:

Understand when and why AI projects need high-performance computing (HPC).
Be able to start a JupyterHub session with GPUs on Isambard-AI.
Be able to prepare an image dataset and train an image classification model on a GPU.
Know how to judge a classifier on imbalanced medical data.
Understand how training a model on multiple GPUs works.
Know how to work considerately on a shared supercomputer.

title: Before the course
text:
0.1 What you’ll need

An Isambard-AI account that has been added to the course project. We’ll email you an invitation before the course; accept it and follow the steps in the email.

title: Getting onto Isambard-AI
text:
Section 2 of 7
On a supercomputer, you don’t run your code on the computer you log in to. Instead, you ask a scheduler for the resources you need, and it finds a free compute node for you. The scheduler on Isambard-AI is called Slurm. JupyterHub talks to Slurm for us and then opens JupyterLab in the browser, running on the node Slurm found.

title: Getting onto Isambard-AI
text:
2.1 Start a session

Go to https://apps.isambard.ac.uk/aip2-jupyter and log in.
Fill in the Server Options form:








Field
What to choose




Project
The course project (we’ll tell you its name)


Job duration
The shortest option that lasts until the end of the course


Number of GH200s
1


Partition
Leave this empty


Reservation
interactive




Click Start. You might see “Pending in queue” while Slurm finds you a node. This is usually quick, but it can take longer if the interactive nodes are busy. JupyterLab opens in your browser once the node is ready.







Your session has a time limit



When the time you chose runs out, the session ends straight away, with no warning. Save your notebook regularly (Ctrl+S or Cmd+S).

title: Getting onto Isambard-AI
text:
2.2 Set up the course kernel
The kernel is the Python environment your notebook runs in. We’ve made one especially for this course, with PyTorch and all the other packages installed, and you need to tell JupyterLab to use it. You only have to do this once.
In JupyterLab, open a terminal (File → New → Terminal) and run:


Terminal

$PROJECTDIR/hpc-ai-1/venv/bin/python -m ipykernel install --user --name hpc-ai-1 --display-name "Python (HPC for AI part 1)"

Then copy the course notebook into your home folder:


Terminal

cp $PROJECTDIR/hpc-ai-1/hpc-for-ai.ipynb ~/

Open hpc-for-ai.ipynb from the file browser on the left. The kernel name in the top right of the notebook should say “Python (HPC for AI part 1)”. If it says something else, click on it and choose that kernel from the list.

title: Getting onto Isambard-AI
text:
2.3 Check your GPUs
Run the first two cells of the notebook. The first one loads the libraries we need:


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

import os
import shutil
import time
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import torch
from IPython.display import Image as ShowImage
from IPython.display import display
from PIL import Image
from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay, classification_report
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Isambard-AI's compute nodes can't reach the internet, so tell Ultralytics
# not to try downloading anything. This must be set before importing it.
os.environ["YOLO_OFFLINE"] = "1"

# Lets training give the same result each time. It has to be set before the
# GPU is first used, which is why it's here at the top.
os.environ["CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG"] = ":4096:8"

from ultralytics import YOLO







Going deeper: the two environment variables





The cell sets two environment variables, which are settings that libraries read when they start up.

YOLO_OFFLINE tells Ultralytics not to try downloading anything (it normally checks for updates and downloads a font and some extra model files). Without it, you’d see warnings about failed downloads, and training would take a little longer to start.
CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG is needed for training to give exactly the same result each time it runs with the same settings. It has to be set before the GPU is first used, otherwise PyTorch prints a long warning during training.




The second cell asks PyTorch which GPUs it can see. It should find one, with a name like NVIDIA GH200.


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

print("PyTorch version:", torch.__version__)
print("CUDA available: ", torch.cuda.is_available())
print("Number of GPUs: ", torch.cuda.device_count())
for i in range(torch.cuda.device_count()):
    print(f"  GPU {i}: {torch.cuda.get_device_name(i)}")

You can also see the GPUs from the terminal with nvidia-smi (the NVIDIA System Management Interface), which lists each GPU, how much of its memory is in use and what’s running on it:


Terminal

nvidia-smi

JupyterLab on Isambard-AI also has a GPU dashboard. Click the GPU icon in the left-hand sidebar, open the GPU Utilization and GPU Memory panels, and keep them somewhere you can see them. You’ll use them to watch the GPUs while the model trains.

title: Getting onto Isambard-AI
text:
2.4 Your first GPU job
To see how much faster a GPU is, the next cell multiplies two large matrices (8,192 × 8,192 numbers each), first on the CPU and then on a GPU, and times both.


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

size = 8192
a = torch.randn(size, size)
b = torch.randn(size, size)

# On the CPU
start = time.perf_counter()
a @ b
cpu_time = time.perf_counter() - start

# On GPU 0
a_gpu = a.to("cuda")
b_gpu = b.to("cuda")
a_gpu @ b_gpu  # warm-up: the first call includes one-off set-up costs
torch.cuda.synchronize()
start = time.perf_counter()
a_gpu @ b_gpu
torch.cuda.synchronize()  # wait for the GPU to finish before stopping the clock
gpu_time = time.perf_counter() - start

print(f"CPU: {cpu_time:.3f} s")
print(f"GPU: {gpu_time:.4f} s")
print(f"The GPU was {cpu_time / gpu_time:.0f}x faster")

A couple of lines need explaining:

.to("cuda") copies the numbers from the CPU’s memory into the GPU’s memory. CUDA is NVIDIA’s platform for running code on its GPUs.
torch.cuda.synchronize() waits for the GPU to finish. Python doesn’t wait for the GPU by default; it carries on as soon as it has sent the work. Without this line we’d be timing how long it took to send the work, rather than how long it took to do it.

We also run the multiplication once on the GPU before we start timing. The first thing you do on a GPU is slower than usual because of one-off setup, and we don’t want that in our timing.

title: Getting onto Isambard-AI
text:
2.5 Where things live
Isambard-AI has several places to store files. We’ll use three of them:








Location
What it is
What we use it for




$PROJECTDIR
Shared by everyone in the project. Not backed up.
The dataset, model weights and course kernel. You can read these but not change them.


$SCRATCHDIR
Your own working space. Not backed up.
Everything you create, including the data split and your trained models.


$HOME
Your home folder, limited to 100 GiB. Not backed up.
Your copy of the notebook.



The compute nodes on Isambard-AI can’t connect to the internet, so everything the notebook needs, including the dataset and the model weights, has been downloaded in advance into the project folder. The next cell sets up the paths to these files, and to your own working folder. It should print True for both the dataset and the model weights.


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

# Shared course files (read-only for you)
COURSE_DIR = Path(os.environ.get("PROJECTDIR", "/projects/b6er")) / "hpc-ai-1"
DATA_DIR = COURSE_DIR / "FracAtlas"
WEIGHTS = COURSE_DIR / "weights" / "yolov8n-cls.pt"

# Your own working folder
WORK_DIR = Path(os.environ.get("SCRATCHDIR", Path.home())) / "hpc-ai-1"
SPLIT_DIR = WORK_DIR / "fracatlas-split"
RUNS_DIR = WORK_DIR / "runs"
WORK_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

print("Dataset found:      ", DATA_DIR.exists(), "-", DATA_DIR)
print("Model weights found:", WEIGHTS.exists(), "-", WEIGHTS)
print("Your work folder:   ", WORK_DIR)

title: Getting onto Isambard-AI
text:
Exercise






Exercise




Run nvidia-smi in a terminal. How much memory does your GPU have, and how much is being used?
Change size to 16384 in the matrix multiplication cell and run it again. Each matrix now has four times as many numbers. How do the CPU and GPU times change?









Show answer






Your session has one GPU, with about 96 GB of memory (nvidia-smi shows it in MiB). Once you’ve run the matrix multiplication cell, it shows some memory in use by your notebook.
Multiplying two n × n matrices takes roughly n³ operations, so doubling size means about 8 times as much work. The CPU time goes up a lot. The GPU time goes up much less, because the GPU has more work to spread across its cores, so the gap between the two usually gets bigger. Your exact numbers will be different.

title: Training on one GPU
text: Section 4 of 7

title: Training on one GPU
text:
4.1 The model
We’ll use YOLOv8n-cls, a small image classification model from the Ultralytics library. It’s a convolutional neural network, a type of neural network that picks out patterns such as edges, textures and shapes in different parts of an image.
To train a model like this from scratch, we’d need far more than 4,000 images. Instead we use transfer learning. We start with a model that has already been trained on more than a million everyday photos (the ImageNet dataset), so it has already learned to recognise general visual patterns, and then we fine-tune it on our X-rays.

title: Training on one GPU
text:
4.2 Training settings


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

EPOCHS = 50
IMG_SIZE = 512
BATCH = 64
WORKERS = 8








Setting
What it means




EPOCHS
The number of times the model sees every training image.


IMG_SIZE
The width and height, in pixels, of the square each image is turned into.


BATCH
The number of images the model looks at before it updates its weights.


WORKERS
The number of CPU processes loading images in the background, so the GPU doesn’t have to wait for them.

title: Training on one GPU
text:
4.3 Train
Open the GPU dashboard before you run the next cell so that you can watch the GPU while the model trains.


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

model = YOLO(WEIGHTS)

start = time.perf_counter()
model.train(
    data=str(SPLIT_DIR),
    epochs=EPOCHS,
    imgsz=IMG_SIZE,
    batch=BATCH,
    workers=WORKERS,
    device=0,  # one GPU
    project=str(RUNS_DIR),
    name="1gpu",
    exist_ok=True,
    seed=42,
)
time_1gpu = time.perf_counter() - start
print(f"Training on 1 GPU took {time_1gpu / 60:.1f} minutes")

device=0 tells Ultralytics to use GPU 0 only. project and name tell it where to save the results, which in this case is runs/1gpu in your scratch folder.
While it’s training, Ultralytics prints a line for each epoch with the loss, which measures how wrong the model is on the training images, and the accuracy on the validation set. The loss should go down and the accuracy should go up.

title: Training on one GPU
text:
4.4 How did training go?
Ultralytics saves some plots of the training run in the run’s folder. This cell shows the main one.


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

run_1gpu = RUNS_DIR / "1gpu"
display(ShowImage(filename=str(run_1gpu / "results.png"), width=800))

Compare the two loss plots. If the training loss keeps falling but the validation loss starts to rise, the model is overfitting: it’s learning details of the training images that don’t help with new ones. You may see this towards the end of our run. This is one reason Ultralytics saves the epoch that did best on the validation set as best.pt, as well as the final one.






Going deeper: the training plots





Each small plot shows one measurement, with the epoch number along the bottom. The blue line is the value at each epoch, and the dotted orange line is a smoothed version that makes the trend easier to see.








Plot
What it shows
What you want to see




train/loss
How wrong the model is on the training images
Going down


val/loss
How wrong the model is on the validation images, which it doesn’t learn from
Going down, then levelling off


metrics/accuracy_top1
The proportion of validation images the model classifies correctly
Going up, then levelling off


metrics/accuracy_top5
Whether the right answer is in the model’s top five guesses
Ignore it: with only two classes, it’s always 1

title: Training on one GPU
text:
4.5 Test the model
The version of the model that did best on the validation set is saved as best.pt. We load it, ask it to classify every image in the test set, and compare its answers with the real labels. * in the path means “anything”, so test/*/*.jpg matches every image in both class folders. The folder each image is in tells us its real label.


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

def evaluate(weights):
    """Classify every test image and return the true and predicted labels."""
    model = YOLO(weights)
    true, pred = [], []
    test_images = str(SPLIT_DIR / "test" / "*" / "*.jpg")  # every image in every class folder
    for result in model.predict(test_images, imgsz=IMG_SIZE, stream=True, verbose=False):
        true.append(Path(result.path).parent.name)  # the folder name is the true label
        pred.append(result.names[result.probs.top1])  # the class the model thinks is most likely
    return true, pred

true, pred = evaluate(run_1gpu / "weights" / "best.pt")
print(classification_report(true, pred, digits=3))

ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(true, pred, cmap="Purples")
plt.title("1 GPU: test set")
plt.show()

classification_report gives three scores for each class:







Score
What it tells us about the fractured class




Precision
When the model says “fractured”, how often is it right?


Recall
What proportion of the real fractures did the model find? This is also called sensitivity.


F1-score
A single score that combines precision and recall.


Support
How many images of that class are in the test set.









Going deeper: the summary rows and the confusion matrix





The rows at the bottom of the report summarise both classes:







Row
What it means




accuracy
The proportion of all test images the model classified correctly.


macro avg
The plain average of the two classes’ scores, so each class counts equally.


weighted avg
The average weighted by support. There are many more not_fractured images, so this is close to the not_fractured scores.



Below the report is a confusion matrix, which compares the model’s answers with the real labels. The real label is up the side and the model’s answer is along the bottom, and each box shows a number of images. The correct answers are on the diagonal, from top left to bottom right. The missed fractures are in the fractured row, not_fractured column, and the false alarms are in the not_fractured row, fractured column.

title: Training on one GPU
text:
4.6 Is that accuracy any good?


hpc-for-ai.ipynb

baseline = (test_df["fractured"] == 0).mean()
print(f"Always guessing 'not fractured' would be {baseline:.1%} accurate")

Most of the images don’t show a fracture, so a “model” that always said “not fractured” would be right over 80% of the time, and it wouldn’t find a single fracture. That’s why accuracy on its own can be misleading when the data is imbalanced.
If we wanted to use this model to decide which scans to look at first, the most important score would be the recall for the fractured class. Missing a fracture is worse than a false alarm that a clinician can check and rule out.

title: Training on one GPU
text:
Exercise






Exercise



Look at the classification report and confusion matrix for your 1-GPU model.

What is the model’s recall for the fractured class? What does that number mean in plain English?
How many of the real fractures in the test set did the model miss?
Would you be happy using this model to decide which X-rays to look at first? What would you want to know before you did?

If you have time: change IMG_SIZE to 224 in the settings cell, then run the training and testing cells again. How do the training time and recall change?








Show answer






Look at the recall value in the fractured row. A recall of 0.70, for example, means the model found 70% of the fractures in the test set and missed the other 30%.
In the confusion matrix, the missed fractures are the images where the true label is fractured but the predicted label is not_fractured.
Almost certainly not yet. You’d want to know, for example, how well it works on X-rays from other hospitals and for each body region, whether it’s taking shortcuts such as spotting hardware, how it does with a proper split by patient, and whether it actually helps in a clinical study. A model like this would only ever support a clinician’s decision, not replace it.

Training should be quite a bit faster with smaller images. Recall may drop, because fine details such as hairline fractures can be lost when the image is made smaller, but with only 108 fractures in the test set, a small difference could just be chance. Remember to set IMG_SIZE back to 512 afterwards.

title: Good practice and next steps
text:
Section 6 of 7
Isambard-AI is used by researchers all over the UK. These habits help it work well for everyone, including you.

title: Good practice and next steps
text:
6.1 Look after your session
Check how much time your session has left by running this in a terminal:


Terminal

squeue --me --partition=interactive --name="spawner-jupyterhub" --format="%.10M %.10L"

TIME is how long your session has been running and TIME_LEFT is how long it has left. You need --partition=interactive because sessions in the interactive reservation don’t show up in squeue --me on its own.
Remember that the session ends without any warning, so save your work regularly. When you’ve finished, stop your server by going to File → Hub Control Panel and clicking Stop My Server. Until you do, the GPUs stay reserved for you even if you aren’t using them, and they count against your project’s allocation.

title: Good practice and next steps
text:
6.2 Look after your data
None of the storage on Isambard-AI is backed up, including $HOME, $SCRATCHDIR and $PROJECTDIR, so copy anything important somewhere safe.

Put large datasets in $PROJECTDIR, so everyone in the project can share one copy, as we did with FracAtlas.
Keep working files, such as checkpoints and outputs, in $SCRATCHDIR rather than $HOME, which is limited to 100 GiB.

title: Good practice and next steps
text:
6.3 Use the GPUs well

Keep an eye on the GPU dashboard. If a GPU is idle a lot of the time, adding more GPUs won’t help. Try more data-loading workers, a bigger batch or a bigger model instead.
Start small. Test your code on one GPU for a few epochs before you ask for more.
Only ask for what you need. If your job only uses one GPU, ask for one GH200 rather than four.

title: Good practice and next steps
section: 6.4 When to move on from notebooks
text:
6.4 When to move on from notebooks
Notebooks are good for exploring data and learning, but they’re not ideal for long training runs. The session has a time limit, and if your browser or internet connection drops, you can lose track of where you were.
For real projects, the next step is to put your training code into a Python script and submit it to Slurm as a batch job. A batch job runs on its own, even after you’ve logged out, and you can queue up lots of runs at once. Our Introduction to HPC course covers how to do this.

title: Good practice and next steps
text:
6.5 Where to go next

Introduction to HPC covers scripts, batch jobs and Slurm.
The Isambard-AI documentation, including the JupyterHub guide.
The BriCS Distributed PyTorch Training tutorial shows how to train across several nodes.
The Ultralytics image classification documentation.
